course_description:
This course examines the long tradition of Australian drama from early convict theatre, through nineteenth century melodrama, and across the bush drama, New Wave, Aboriginal drama and 'Internationalist' schools of the twentieth century to the present day. Questions the course asks include 'How is national identity reflected in the theatre Australia produces?', or even more importantly, 'How is national identity shaped by the work of theatre-makers across time?'

This course traces the development of a distinctive Australian voice in theatre and drama from its origins in late C19th melodrama to the present. The first four weeks of the course comprise an Australian Gothic drama module that spans from the convict era through to the present day and also examines the burgeoning Blak Gothic theatre movement. The rest of the course then tracks a chronological pathway covering topics such as urban theatre, the New Wave, Indigenous theatre, and then a range of the most exciting plays and theatre trends of the late C20th and early C21st. The course thus traces a cultural and political history of Australia from British colonisation to the present, emphasising the integral role theatre plays in not only reflecting, but also helping to shape issues of national identity. In addition to an increased appreciation and understanding of an Australian national theatre canon, students are consequently expected to come out of this course with an increased understanding and appreciation of Australian national historiesﾠand identities.

course_aims:
This course aims to provide students with an intimate knowledge and appreciation of a national Australian theatre canon, as well developing the critical reasoning to question and challenge the very notion of canonicity itself, by examining theatre from the convict era to the present.

Students will explore broader over-arching themes and topics in Australian theatre and its tropes through tutorial work and performance, by attending live theatre, and through individual and/or collaborative performative research.

The course thus aims to instill in students a sense of 'narrative' not only of the history of Australian theatre from the late C18th to the present; but also to question and challengeﾠissues of national identity during the same period. The course inextricably links issues of national cultural and political identity with the theatre and drama being produced at any given time. To understand Australian drama is to better understand the culture that produced it.

As well as developing knowledge of theatre history and its themes, students are also expected to develop a knowledge of changing theatrical practices over the past two centuries.

Key topics covered in this course include: Australian Gothic drama, urban theatre, national political and cultural identity, Indigenous and multicultural theatre, queer and contemporary drama.

Queensland-specific independent and mainstage theatre practice will also be placed in conversation with the national repertoire where appropriate.

learning_outcomes.description: Articulate an understanding of an Australian (and, where appropriate, Queensland-specific) theatre canon from British settlement/invasion/colonisation to the present including Indigenous perspectives.
Articulate an understanding of how Australian theatre engages with, reflects and helps shape issues of national identity.
Understand how Australian drama differs from and/or complements cultural expression taking place in other forms, such as film, television and literature.
Develop an understanding of an Australian theatrical canon both through independent learning and through group work, where appropriate.

assessment_details.title: Research Essay
assessment_details.task_description: The research essay is designed to enable you to demonstrate your acquired knowledge and research skills by writing on a specific aspect of Australian Gothic drama in relation to one of the key concepts, movements, texts or figures arising from weeks two to four. This task will assess your ability to: answer a relevant and compelling research question provide an analytic approach to the topic and its relevant issues construct a strong argument provide evidence from the text (where appropriate) and/or secondary material to support this argument. The referencing style used for Drama assignments is MLA 9th edition. Detailed instructions for this assignment will be distributed in class and posted on Blackboard at the beginning of semester. Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Machine Translation (MT) are emerging tools that may support students in completing this assessment task. Students may appropriately use AI and/or MT in completing this assessment task. Students must clearly reference any use of AI or MT in each instance. A failure to reference generative AI or MT use may constitute student misconduct under the Student Code of Conduct. Read full task description Hide full task description

assessment_details.title: 10 Minute Group Performances
assessment_details.task_description: In a small group (4-6 students), deliver a 10-minute group performance to the class on one of the following plays comprising the late twentieth and early twenty-first century sections of the course: Summer of the Seventeenth Doll, The Season at Sarsaparilla by Patrick White, White With Wire Wheels by Jack Hibberd, Historia by Noelle Janaczewska, Single Asian Female by Michelle Law, Hubris and Humiliation by Lewis Treston. This is a group performance project. Group members will each receive the same grade out of 30 for the performance. The performances will take place during your tutorial slot in Week 12 of semester. A full assignment brief will be provided in Blackboard during the semester. Group performances will take place in the Avalon Theatre. Recording of Oral and Practical Assessment All presentations will be recorded for marking purposes via recording facilities available where the assessment takes place (eg. ECHO360, Zoom, camera device) Recordings will be retained by the School of Communication and Arts for at least 12 months from the release of the final grade for the course. Recordings will be stored in a secure manner and will only be accessed by authorised school staff for the purposes of: Moderation of marking; Provision of feedback to the student(s) recorded; and/or Re-marking following a successful re-mark application. learning_activities.topic: Week 1 - Introduction to Australian Drama Overview of the course and a chronological overview of Australian theatre history from the convict era to the present. Learning outcomes: L01, L02
Week 1 - No tutorials

Week 2 - Bush Gothic Drama The lecture will provide students with an introduction to Australian Gothic drama, defining key terms, before turning to early twentieth-century genre, Bush Gothic and its more recent postcolonial rejoinders. Holy Day by Andrew Bovell is the set text. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03

Week 2 - Bush Gothic Drama Tutorials will be devoted to discussing and activating the set performance text ( Holy Day ) for this week, and engaging with discussion of key terms, lecture content and other set or recommended reading. Learning outcomes: L01, L03, L04
Week 3 - Ekka Public Holiday - no classes this week No classes this week as our Wednesday lecture and tutorial fall on the Ekka Public Holiday.

Week 4 - Contemporary Gothic Drama This lecture provides an overview of Australian Gothic drama from the late twentieth century through to the present, using the set text ( Mortido by Angela Betzien) as the contemporary example. Learning outcomes: L01, L03, L04

Week 4 - Contemporary Gothic Drama Tutorials will be devoted to discussing and activating the set performance text ( Mortido ) for this week, and engaging with discussion of key terms, lecture content and other set or recommended reading. Learning outcomes: L01, L03, L04

Week 5 - Blak Gothic Drama The lecture provides an overview of the burgeoning Australian theatre genre of Blak Gothic drama, using the set text ( The Drover's Wife by Leah Purcell) as a contemporary example. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03

Week 5 - Blak Gothic Drama Tutorials will be devoted to discussing and activating the set performance text ( The Drover's Wife ) for this week, and engaging with discussion of key terms, lecture content and other set or recommended reading. Learning outcomes: L01, L03, L04

Week 6 - Urban Drama The lecture provides an overview of the rise of Australian drama with an urban setting in the postwar period of the 1950s, using Ray Lawler's Summer of the Seventeenth Doll as the exemplar. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03

Week 6 - Urban Drama Tutorials will be devoted to discussing and activating the set performance text ( Summer of the Seventeenth Doll ) for this week, and engaging with discussion of key terms, lecture content and other set or recommended reading. Learning outcomes: L01, L03, L04

Week 7 - Suburban Drama The lecture provides an overview of the rise of Australian suburbia in the 1950s and 1960s, which the set text (Patrick White's The Season at Sarsaparilla ) satirises. The rise of federal arts funding and the professionalisation of state theatre companies is also discussed. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03

Week 7 - Suburban Drama Tutorials will be devoted to discussing and activating the set performance text ( The Season at Sarsaparilla ) for this week, and engaging with discussion of key terms, lecture content and other set or recommended reading. Learning outcomes: L01, L03, L04

Week 8 - The New Wave The lecture examines the New Wave theatre movement of the 1960s and 1970s. Topics discussed include its urban focus in Sydney and Melbourne (with a brief inclusion of what was happening in Brisbane during this time), and who the movement excluded. Jack Hibberd's White with Wire Wheels is the set text. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03

Week 8 - The New Wave Tutorials will be devoted to discussing and activating the set performance text ( White with Wire Wheels ) for this week, and engaging with discussion of key terms, lecture content and other set or recommended reading. Learning outcomes: L01, L03, L04

Week 9 - Indigenous Drama This lecture provides an overview of Indigenous drama from its rise in the 1970s through to the present day, examining its changing characteristics over time. Where possible, an Indigenous theatre artist will be invited to provide personal insights and observations. Jack Davis's The Dreamers is the set text. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03

Week 9 - Indigenous Drama Tutorials will be devoted to discussing and activating the set performance text ( The Dreamers ) for this week, and engaging with discussion of key terms, lecture content and other set or recommended reading. Learning outcomes: L01, L03, L04
MID-SEMESTER BREAK No lectures or tutorials during the mid-semester break.

Week 10 - The 1990s: Queer goes Mainstream The lecture provides an overview of the internationalisation of Australian theatre during the 1990s and its increasing inclusion of voices that were marginal to the mainstage in previous decades. Noelle Janaczewska's Historia is the set text. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03

Week 10 - The 1990s: Queer goes Mainstream Tutorials will be devoted to discussing and activating the set performance text ( Historia ) for this week, and engaging with discussion of key terms, lecture content and other set or recommended reading. Learning outcomes: L01, L03, L04

Week 11 - Contemporary Australian Drama 1 This week's lecture provides an overview of the 21st century explosion of diversity on stage and the rise of young playwrights-of-colour. Single Asian Female by Michelle Law is the set text. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03

Week 11 - Contemporary Australian Drama 1 Tutorials will be devoted to discussing and activating the set performance text ( Single Asian Female ) for this week, and engaging with discussion of key terms, lecture content and other set or recommended reading. . Learning outcomes: L01, L03, L04

Week 12 - Contemporary Australian Drama 2: Writing back to the canon Final lecture! We finish the course with a new classic that rewrites and revisions the theatrical and literary canon. Lewis Treston's camp homage to Jane Austen, Hubris and Humiliation, is the set text. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03
Week 12 - Group Performances Group performances take place during your regular tutorial slot. Learning outcomes: L04
Week 13- No Lecture No classes
Week 13- No tutorials No classes

policies_and_procedures: University policies and procedures apply to all aspects of student life. As a UQ student, you must comply with University-wide and program-specific requirements, including the: Student Code of Conduct Policy Student Integrity and Misconduct Policy and Procedure Assessment Procedure Examinations Procedure Reasonable Adjustments for Students Policy and Procedure AI for Assessment Guide Recording of Teaching Policy and Procedure Learn more about UQ policies on my.UQ and the Policy and Procedure Library . Course guidelines Communication Expectations While you are a student at UQ, all communication must be conducted according to the UQ Student Code of Conduct . The UQ Library has a helpful Communicate and collaborate online module . Email is the primary way for you to send messages to, and receive information from, the School and our staff. You must use your UQ email address (not a private address) to communicate with staff. You should add a clear subject line, including course code, and a 2-3 word statement. You can send email at any time, however, please do not expect responses outside normal working hours (Monday to Friday from ~8am to ~5pm). Emails that constitute bullying, harassment or discrimination against staff contravene the Student Code of Conduct. Emails like this will be reported to the University, and the matter will be pursued as misconduct. Learning activities
